newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuanians vote with Landsbergis eyeing return.
newsitem.headline: Lithuanians vote with Landsbergis eyeing return.

text.p: Lithuanians on Sunday voted for a new parliament for the second time since quitting the former Soviet Union with the right wing, led by independence hero Vytautas Landsbergis, eyeing a return to power.

Landsbergis was snubbed at the polls four years ago as Lithuanians, reeling from the economic collapse that followed independence, propelled the ex-Communists of the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP) into power.
Turnout this time was lower than in 1992 in the battle for a parliament where remnants of graffiti-covered barricades still stand as a reminder of the independence struggle.
Election officials said some 30 percent of voters had cast their ballots by mid-afternoon, indicating the final turnout would be down on the high 75 percent showing four years ago.
Political commentators said many Lithuanians have become disillusioned by politics, in stark contrast to the euphoria of independence days.
The stocky and bespectacled Landsbergis was the unlikely driving force of Lithuania's independence fight and is now hoping to come back to power as head of the Homeland Union.
"I would like to serve again in a more important position as I see that my work is unfinished and damaged in many ways," he told Reuters in an interview in his party's busy headquarters.
He won many admirers for himself and the Lithuanian people as they stood up to the might of the former Soviet Union.

But as economic chaos and soaring inflation beset the country after independence, Lithuanians dumped his Sajudis movement at the ballot box for the familiar faces of the LDLP, the revamped Communist party.
The LDLP sealed its return to power as its leader Algirdas Brazauskas won presidential elections the year after.
But Landsbergis went into Sunday's elections with a good chance of revenge as his Homeland Union Party held a lead in opinion polls.
Polls suggested his group would be the largest party in the 141-seat parliament but would have to form a coalition government.
Although the LDLP produced macroeconomic gains and followed a strongly pro-Western policy, many Lithuanians accuse them of reneging on their populist promises and of corruption and croneyism.
The ex-Communists were also badly hurt at the end of last year when a former prime minister withdrew his personal savings from a bank days before it was shut at the start of a banking crisis.
Brazauskas, a broad-shouldered former engineer who now has no party affiliation, said he hoped a new government would not mean dramatic changes in Lithuania's course.
The Homeland Union has said it will work with the Christian Democrats to form the core of a new coalition but analysts say it is not clear which other parties they can work with.
"The main thing is that we must have thoughtful people, who consider the future and not just their own political ambitions," Brazauksas told reporters after voting.
